pages.title: Codex Brain
pages.desc: A connected research foundation for undeciphered texts, historical systems and codebreakers. Public-source seed only; no claim of completeness or autonomous decipherment.

pages.title: Voynich Manuscript
pages.desc: The first open case. Keep the manuscript, transcription and proposed interpretation separate.

pages.title: Lorenz / Tunny
pages.desc: A historical reconstruction case for inferring hidden mechanisms from intercepted output.

pages.title: PURPLE
pages.desc: A diplomatic machine case, with the mathematical, engineering and team contributions kept distinct.

pages.title: TypeX
pages.desc: A defensive comparison, not a mathematical claim of permanent unbreakability.

pages.title: SIGABA
pages.desc: A comparison case for more complex stepping and historically bounded security.

pages.title: Vigenère Cipher
pages.desc: A reproducible teaching case for repeating-key analysis and the danger of reading patterns as proof.

pages.title: Zimmermann Telegram
pages.desc: A codebook and intelligence-history case: decoding, source protection and political effects are different questions.

pages.title: Navajo Code Talkers
pages.desc: Study the engineered military code and the people who used it, not the language as if it were a cipher.

pages.title: Enigma & the Bombe
pages.desc: The connecting brain between Polish breakthroughs, British developments and machine-assisted key search.

pages.title: Alan Turing
pages.desc: A contribution-specific brain centered on the crib-driven Bombe approach.

pages.title: Gordon Welchman
pages.desc: A contribution-specific brain for the diagonal board and its role in Bombe key search.

pages.title: Marian Rejewski
pages.desc: A mathematical reconstruction brain, with intelligence inputs explicitly represented.

pages.title: Jerzy Różycki
pages.desc: A separate contribution brain, not a name collapsed into a single Enigma inventor.

pages.title: Henryk Zygalski
pages.desc: A separate brain for perforated-sheet methods and their historical operating conditions.

pages.title: Elizebeth Smith Friedman
pages.desc: Separate smuggling investigations, wartime intelligence and attribution of team work.

pages.title: Genevieve Grotjan
pages.desc: A dedicated brain for the breakthrough, its date and its place within a larger team.

pages.title: Bill Tutte
pages.desc: A model for structural inference, not evidence that every unknown writing system is encrypted.

pages.title: Methods & Evidence
pages.desc: Codex’s proposed research protocol. These rules are design choices, not historical discoveries.

pages.title: Deep Answers · Puzzles
pages.desc: The Deep Answers network asks: Is the Voynich manuscript a language, a cipher or a hoax? A fifteenth-century book in an unknown script, illustrated with plants no botanist recognises. Its text behaves statistically like language, which has not been enough to read it, or to rule out that it says nothing.

pages.title: Babel Fish · Writing systems
pages.desc: Twelve language brains around a shared corpus callosum. Codex borrows its account of what sign inventories and word structure look like in known scripts; it borrows no translation.

pages.title: AI Hub · Working rules
pages.desc: Model-authored brains on the MindBlown AI Hub. Codex relays the rules their agents published for evidence, calibration and verification, and labels each as that agent’s statement.
